result: Human intestinal epithelial cells (IECs) preferentially produce IFN-λ over IFN-β in response to RNA PAMP stimulation in a MAVS-dependent manner. HT-29 cells expressed 40-60 fold more IFNL3 mRNA and 31-34 fold more IFN-λ protein than IFNB in response to poly(I:C) or RV infection, and this production was completely abolished in MAVS-/- cells. Human ileum enteroids showed similar preferential IFN-λ expression (50-fold higher IFNL3 than IFNB) following RV or VSV infection.
evaluation: Claims C26-C31 are well-supported by data in Figure 1A-C showing consistent preferential IFN-λ expression in multiple human IEC models (HT-29 cells and primary enteroids) and complete dependence on MAVS. The quantitative measurements are specific and reproducible across different stimuli (poly(I:C), RV, VSV). The conclusion that this is an IEC-specific feature is supported by comparison with HEK293 cells.

result: Simian RV RRV replication is enhanced approximately 10-fold in MAVS-/- HT-29 cells compared to wild-type cells, while human RV Wa strain replication is not significantly affected by MAVS deletion. This differential effect was observed both for intracellular viral RNA levels and infectious virus in supernatants.
evaluation: Claims C32-C34 are supported by data in Figure 2A showing clear differential effects of MAVS deletion on RRV versus Wa replication in HT-29 cells. The 10-fold enhancement for RRV and lack of enhancement for Wa is consistent with the host-range restriction hypothesis. Statistical significance is indicated and measurements include both RNA levels and infectious virus titers.

result: RV infection induces specific degradation of full-length MAVS in a strain-dependent and host-species-matched manner. Simian RRV degrades MAVS in simian MA104 cells, human Wa degrades MAVS in human HT-29 cells, and murine ETD degrades MAVS in murine NIH3T3 cells. The degradation is specific to FL-MAVS (not mini-MAVS) and occurs post-transcriptionally without affecting MAVS mRNA levels.
evaluation: Claims C35-C41 are strongly supported by western blot data in Figure 2B-C and supplementary figures showing time-dependent, MOI-dependent, and strain-specific MAVS degradation across multiple cell types. The specificity for FL-MAVS over mini-MAVS and other signaling molecules is clearly demonstrated. The host-range restriction pattern is consistent across three different host-virus pairs. RT-qPCR data confirms post-transcriptional regulation.

result: RV-mediated MAVS degradation functionally blocks IFN signaling, requires active viral replication, and occurs via the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway. RRV infection diminished IFN and ISG promoter activity, UV-inactivated or antibody-neutralized virus did not degrade MAVS, and only proteasome inhibitors (not lysosome or caspase inhibitors) rescued MAVS levels.
evaluation: Claims C42-C45 are well-supported by functional data (Figure 2E showing reduced luciferase from IFN promoters), control experiments with inactivated virus (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), and comprehensive inhibitor screening (Figure 2F and supplement 1F). The conclusion that degradation is proteasome-mediated is based on rescue by three different proteasome inhibitors but not by other pathway inhibitors among ~50 compounds tested.

result: RV VP3, not NSP1, mediates MAVS degradation. Expression of VP3 alone is sufficient to degrade endogenous MAVS in a dose-dependent manner. Reassortant viruses encoding VP3 from specific strains recapitulate the host-range-restricted MAVS degradation pattern observed with parental viruses.
evaluation: Claims C46-C50 are strongly supported by multiple complementary approaches: screening of all 12 RV proteins (Figure 3A), dose-response with ectopic VP3 expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), and genetic evidence from reassortant viruses (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B). The reassortant data provides particularly strong genetic evidence that VP3 is necessary and sufficient for the phenotype. The conclusion is drawn from converging lines of evidence.

result: VP3 physically interacts with MAVS. VP3 was specifically enriched in MAVS immunoprecipitates from MG132-treated infected cells by mass spectrometry, and direct VP3-MAVS interaction was confirmed by co-immunoprecipitation with ectopically expressed proteins and with purified recombinant proteins.
evaluation: Claims C51-C52 are supported by multiple independent interaction assays: IP-MS from infected cells (Figure 3C), co-IP with ectopic expression (Figure 3D), and co-IP with purified recombinant proteins (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C). The convergence of these three different approaches provides strong evidence for direct physical interaction. NSP4 served as an appropriate negative control.

result: The N-terminal 171 amino acids of VP3 are necessary and sufficient for mitochondrial localization, MAVS interaction, and MAVS degradation. The C-terminal phosphodiesterase (PDE) domain and its enzymatic activity are not required for MAVS degradation, as neither PDE inhibitors nor catalytic site mutations (H718A, H797A) rescued MAVS levels.
evaluation: Claims C53-C59 are well-supported by domain mapping experiments (Figure 3E-G), immunofluorescence localization (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), co-IP with deletion mutants (Figure 3F), and both pharmacological and genetic inactivation of PDE activity (Figure 3G and supplement 1E). The data clearly delineate functional domains and rule out PDE activity as the mechanism. The N-terminal domain is both necessary (deletion abolishes activity) and sufficient (expression alone causes degradation).

result: VP3-MAVS interaction is host-range restricted and mediated by the VP3 N-terminus. Simian VP3 interacts with simian MAVS but not with murine or human MAVS. Replacing the N-terminal 171 amino acids of simian VP3 with the corresponding murine sequence completely abolishes interaction with simian MAVS. VP3-mediated degradation is proteasome-dependent.
evaluation: Claims C60-C63 are supported by species-specific co-IP experiments (Figure 3H) and domain-swap experiments showing that the N-terminus determines species specificity (Figure 3H). The proteasome dependence is confirmed by MG132 rescue (Figure 3I). These data provide a molecular explanation for the host-range restriction observed at the viral level and identify the N-terminus as the specificity determinant.

result: Multiple MAVS domains are required for efficient VP3-mediated degradation. While the CARD-PRR region is sufficient for VP3 interaction, efficient degradation requires both the N-terminal CARD-PRR region and the C-terminal transmembrane domain that mediates mitochondrial localization. CARD-PRR-EGFP-TM is degraded as efficiently as full-length MAVS, while CARD-PRR-EGFP or EGFP-TM alone are stable.
evaluation: Claims C64-C67 are supported by systematic domain deletion analysis (Figure 4A-C) showing differential stability of MAVS fragments during RV infection. The data clearly demonstrate that interaction (via CARD-PRR) is necessary but not sufficient, and that mitochondrial localization (via TM) is also required. This suggests a two-step model where VP3 binds MAVS and then requires mitochondrial context for degradation.

result: Lysine 10 in the MAVS CARD domain is critical for VP3-mediated degradation and MAVS is modified by K48-linked polyubiquitination during RV infection. K10A mutation partially rescues MAVS from degradation, and this residue is highly conserved across species. K48-polyubiquitin linkage is consistent with proteasomal degradation.
evaluation: Claims C68-C71 are supported by mutagenesis data (Figure 4D and supplement 1A) showing that K10 mutations provide partial protection from degradation, and by ubiquitin linkage-specific IP experiments (Figure 4E) demonstrating K48-polyubiquitination. The K48 linkage is the canonical signal for proteasomal degradation, consistent with the inhibitor data. The partial rescue suggests K10 is important but other residues may also contribute.

result: VP3 mediates phosphorylation of a novel SPLTSS motif (residues 188-193) in the MAVS proline-rich region, and this phosphorylation is essential for MAVS degradation. Mass spectrometry identified phosphorylation of two serines and one threonine within this motif (totaling 16% of MAVS proteins) during RV infection. Mutation of the SPLTSS motif to six alanines completely abolished RV-induced MAVS degradation, while mutation of three methylated arginines had no effect.
evaluation: Claims C72-C78 are strongly supported by high-resolution IP-MS data (Figure 4F) identifying novel phosphorylation sites, and by mutagenesis experiments (Figure 4G and supplement 1C) showing complete protection from degradation when the SPLTSS motif is mutated. The specificity is demonstrated by the lack of effect of arginine mutations. The phosphorylation is detected both during infection and with VP3 expression alone (though data not shown for the latter). This represents discovery of a novel regulatory motif.

result: VP3-MAVS interaction occurs independently of the SPLTSS phosphorylation motif, and MAVS mutants (SPLTSS and K7RK10R) retain full IFN-inducing activity. VP3 from human RV binds human MAVS but not simian MAVS, and this binding is not affected by mutation of either the SPLTSS motif or the arginine methylation sites.
evaluation: Claims C79-C81 are supported by co-IP experiments with MAVS mutants (Figure 4H) showing that binding is independent of the phosphorylation motif, and by functional assays (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) showing that the mutants retain IFN-inducing capacity. This establishes a sequential model: VP3 first binds MAVS (independent of SPLTSS), then mediates phosphorylation of SPLTSS, leading to ubiquitination and degradation. The mutants are functional, ruling out misfolding artifacts.

result: VP3-mediated MAVS degradation occurs in vivo during RV infection of mouse intestinal epithelial cells. Murine EW RV infection decreased MAVS protein levels in sorted IECs without affecting Mavs mRNA levels, while simian RRV did not degrade murine MAVS. Despite higher replication, EW induced less IFN-λ than RRV, consistent with MAVS inhibition.
evaluation: Claims C82-C84 are supported by western blot analysis of sorted IECs from infected mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), RT-qPCR showing stable Mavs transcripts (supplement 1B), and IFN-λ measurements (supplement 1C). The in vivo data recapitulates the in vitro findings and demonstrates physiological relevance. The inverse correlation between virus replication and IFN induction for EW versus RRV supports the functional significance of MAVS degradation.

result: MAVS deficiency selectively enhances heterologous (simian RRV) but not homologous (murine EW) RV replication in vivo. RRV fecal shedding increased 1-2 logs in Mavs-/- mice compared to wild-type, and intestinal and hepatic RRV replication were significantly enhanced. In contrast, EW replication was similar between wild-type and Mavs-/- mice.
evaluation: Claims C85-C90 are strongly supported by comprehensive in vivo data including fecal shedding over 12 days (Figure 5A) and tissue viral loads at multiple time points and anatomical sites (Figure 5B). The selective enhancement of RRV but not EW replication in Mavs-/- mice provides strong genetic evidence that VP3-mediated MAVS degradation contributes to viral pathogenesis. The magnitude of effect (100-fold) is substantial and statistically significant.

result: Heterologous simian RRV replication is substantially restricted by both MAVS-IFN signaling and inflammasome-mediated pyroptosis in vivo. RRV replication increased approximately 100-fold in Ifnar1-/-, Mavs-/-, Casp1-/-, and Nlrp9b-/- mice but not in Il18-/- mice, indicating that pyroptosis (cell death) rather than IL-18 secretion mediates viral restriction.
evaluation: Claims C91, C93, and C94 are supported by comparative analysis across multiple knockout mouse strains (Figure 5C). The similar magnitude of enhancement in Mavs-/-, Casp1-/-, and Nlrp9b-/- mice indicates comparable contributions of IFN and inflammasome pathways. The lack of effect in Il18-/- mice specifically implicates pyroptosis over cytokine secretion. This represents an important mechanistic insight into antiviral defense mechanisms in the intestine.

result: Peroxisome-localized MAVS (pex-MAVS) induces both IFN-λ and IFN-β expression to a similar degree as wild-type and mitochondria-localized MAVS, while mini-MAVS is defective in IFN induction. This was demonstrated in MAVS-/- HEK293 cells reconstituted with different MAVS variants.
evaluation: Claims C95-C96 are supported by reconstitution experiments in MAVS-/- cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) showing that pex-MAVS activates both type I and III IFNs comparably to WT and mito-MAVS, while mini-MAVS is defective. This addresses a controversy in the literature about pex-MAVS function. The data are clear, though the authors note this may be context-dependent. The mini-MAVS result is consistent with prior literature.

result: Background claims establishing the importance of MAVS in antiviral immunity, RV biology, and prior knowledge about viral antagonism of MAVS. These include: MAVS is critical for RNA sensing and IFN induction; Mavs-/- mice are susceptible to multiple RNA viruses; multiple viruses target MAVS for degradation; RVs infect intestinal epithelial cells in a host-range-restricted manner; and type I and III IFNs restrict heterologous RV replication.
evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C11-C20, C22-C25 are background/context claims supported by citations to established literature. These provide the scientific foundation and rationale for the study but are not novel findings from this work. They are appropriately cited and accurately represent prior knowledge in the field.

result: Summary of the main findings stated in the abstract: VP3 degrades MAVS in a host-range-restricted manner through phosphorylation of the SPLTSS motif, leading to proteasomal degradation and blockade of IFN-λ production, which contributes to enhanced RV replication and pathogenesis in vivo.
evaluation: Claims C4-C10 are high-level summary statements from the abstract that are supported by the detailed experimental results described in the other claim groups. These represent the main conclusions of the paper and are well-supported by the comprehensive data presented throughout the manuscript including cell culture experiments, biochemical analyses, and in vivo studies.

result: VP3 expression during RV infection induces specific degradation of full-length functional MAVS but not the truncated mini-MAVS that does not activate IFN signaling.
evaluation: Claim C21 is supported by western blot data in Figure 2B showing differential degradation of FL-MAVS versus mini-MAVS during RV infection at different MOIs and time points. The specificity for FL-MAVS is consistent throughout the manuscript and represents an important mechanistic detail about the selectivity of VP3-mediated degradation.

result: The suppressive effect of Nlrp9b on RV fecal shedding is more profound for heterologous simian RV than for homologous murine RV.
evaluation: Claim C92 is supported by citation to prior work (Zhu et al., 2017) and is consistent with the data in Figure 5C showing substantial RRV enhancement in Nlrp9b-/- mice. This represents an important comparative observation about differential host restriction mechanisms for homologous versus heterologous viruses.
